title: A MAN MARRIED HIS OWN AUNT—AND GOD CHOSE THEIR SONS TO STAND BEFORE HIM AS PRIESTS.
paragraphs: A MAN MARRIED HIS OWN AUNT—AND GOD CHOSE THEIR SONS TO STAND BEFORE HIM AS PRIESTS.

One of the most uncomfortable family revelations in Exodus is hiding in a genealogy most Christians skip. But behind this controversial marriage lies a breathtaking story of imperfect ancestry, divine deliverance, holy judgment, and the grace that ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
What if I told you that two of the most important men in Israel's spiritual history were born from a marriage that would later be expressly forbidden by God's Law?
Not a rumor.
Not an accusation invented by enemies of the Bible.
Not something hidden in an ancient manuscript that the Church desperately wants to keep secret.
It is written in Scripture.
And once you see it, you may never read the story of Moses and Aaron quite the same way again.
Because behind the burning bush, behind the plagues of Egypt, behind the parting of the Red Sea, behind the golden calf, and behind the sacred garments of Israel's first high priest...
There was a family history that would make many religious people uncomfortable.
A man named Amram married a woman named Jochebed.
She became the mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.
But there was something about their marriage that most Sunday school lessons never mention.
Jochebed was Amram's aunt.
His father's sister.
And the Bible does not attempt to conceal it.
Exodus 6:20 declares:
"And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years." — Exodus 6:20, KJV
Read that again.
His father's sister.
Not his distant cousin.
Not simply a woman from the same tribe.
His aunt.
And from that marriage came Aaron, who became Israel's first high priest, and Moses, who served as Israel's great deliverer, covenant mediator, and priestly intercessor.
Moses himself is also described as exercising priestly ministry in Psalm 99:6, alongside Aaron and Samuel.
But here is where the story becomes even more unsettling.
The very relationship that produced Moses and Aaron would later be explicitly prohibited under the Law delivered through Moses.
Leviticus 18:12 says:
"Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister: she is thy father's near kinswoman." — KJV
And Leviticus 20:19 reinforces the prohibition against sexual relations with one's aunt.
Think about that.
The man through whom God delivered Israel's Law was born into a marriage that the same Law would later prohibit.
The man who confronted Pharaoh...
The man who stood before the burning bush...
The man who lifted his staff over the sea...
The man who ascended Mount Sinai...
Had a family story that some people today would use to discredit him before ever listening to his message.
And yet God called him.
But before we rush to turn this into a comfortable message about how God uses imperfect people, we need to understand something critically important.
God's decision to use someone does not mean God approves of everything in that person's history.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible is not a collection of stories about flawless people who earned God's attention.
It is the revelation of a holy God working through a deeply fallen human world, bringing His redemptive promises to fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And the story of Amram and Jochebed gives us a remarkable glimpse into that truth.
The Hebrew text of Exodus 6:20 is even more direct.
"וַיִּקַּח עַמְרָם אֶת־יוֹכֶבֶד דֹּדָתוֹ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה"
Vayyiqqaḥ ʿAmrām ʾet-Yokheved dodato lo leʾishah.
In natural English:
"And Amram took Jochebed, his aunt, as his wife."
The important Hebrew word is דֹּדָתוֹ (dodato), meaning "his aunt."
There is no need to soften it.
No need to invent another family relationship.
No need to pretend the passage says something more acceptable.
Exodus 6:20 identifies Jochebed as Amram's aunt, and Exodus 6:18 identifies Kohath as Amram's father. Numbers 26:59 also places Jochebed within the family of Levi.
The biblical evidence is straightforward.
And that raises the question many readers are already thinking.
How could God use a family born from such a relationship?
To answer that, we must remember when this marriage occurred.
Amram and Jochebed lived before the giving of the Mosaic Law at Sinai.
The explicit prohibition found in Leviticus had not yet been delivered to Israel as part of that covenant legislation.
This does not mean that every relationship before Sinai was morally acceptable, or that the absence of a written prohibition automatically made something righteous.
Scripture does not give us enough information to declare God's moral assessment of Amram and Jochebed's marriage at the time it occurred.
And we must not claim certainty where God has not spoken.
But we can say this with confidence.
The Bible records their marriage without explicitly praising it, and God later established a clear prohibition against such unions for Israel.
The description of a biblical event is not automatically a divine endorsement of it.
That principle protects us from twisting Scripture to justify behavior God has forbidden.
Yet something else is equally important.
The circumstances of someone's birth do not determine whether that person can receive God's mercy or be called into His service.
Moses and Aaron did not choose the circumstances of their conception.
They did not choose their parents.
They did not write their genealogy.
And God did not treat their ancestry as an automatic disqualification from His redemptive purposes.
That is where this ancient story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because perhaps you did not come from a family whose history could be displayed proudly for everyone to admire.
Perhaps there are things in your family that nobody discusses at reunions.
A relationship that broke the household.
An affair that destroyed trust.
A parent who disappeared.
A pregnancy surrounded by shame.
A secret that everybody knows but nobody dares to mention.
Perhaps your childhood was marked by decisions you never made, consequences you never deserved, and wounds you were too young to understand.
And somewhere along the way, you began believing that your family's history had already written your future.
That because your beginning was complicated, your life would always be disqualified.
But look again at Moses.
He did not enter the world carrying a spotless family résumé.
He entered a world of slavery, oppression, and a royal decree of death.
And before he could speak a single word, his life was already in danger.
Exodus 2 tells us that his mother hid him for three months because Pharaoh had commanded the death of Hebrew baby boys.
Imagine Jochebed holding that child.
Every cry potentially dangerous.
Every passing Egyptian soldier a threat.
Every sunrise another day she might lose him.
The Bible does not record her private prayers, so we should not invent them.
But it does tell us what she did.
She hid her son.
And when she could hide him no longer, she placed him in a basket among the reeds by the Nile.
A mother who had carried a child in her womb now had to place him beyond her arms.
Can you imagine the helplessness of that moment?
She could protect him only so far.
She could not control the river.
She could not control Pharaoh.
She could not control who would discover the basket.
And yet, in the astonishing providence of God, Pharaoh's own daughter found the child.
Moses' sister watched nearby.
And the child was eventually returned to his own mother to be nursed before growing up in Pharaoh's household.
The empire that had ordered his death became the household in which he was raised.
The baby who should have been killed would one day confront the ruler of Egypt.
The child hidden from Pharaoh would become the man sent by God to say:
"Let my people go." — Exodus 5:1, KJV
The river that was supposed to swallow Hebrew sons became the place where Israel's future deliverer was preserved.
But notice something.
God did not merely preserve Moses.
He also raised up Aaron.
Aaron would become Moses' spokesman before Pharaoh, and later he would be consecrated as Israel's first high priest.
Exodus 28:1 records God's command to bring Aaron and his sons near for priestly service.
And suddenly the family genealogy becomes even more extraordinary.
From the household of Amram and Jochebed came the man who led Israel out of Egypt and the man appointed to represent Israel in the priesthood.
Yet Scripture refuses to let us turn either man into a flawless hero.
Moses killed an Egyptian and fled into the wilderness.
Later, even after years of faithful service, he dishonored God at Meribah and was not permitted to lead Israel into the Promised Land (Numbers 20:7–12).
Aaron participated in the making of the golden calf while Moses was on Mount Sinai (Exodus 32).
Yes.
The very man appointed to become Israel's high priest was involved in one of the nation's most infamous acts of idolatry.
Think about the weight of that.
A complicated family beginning.
A miraculous deliverance.
A divine calling.
And still, devastating human failure.
If the Bible were merely a public relations campaign for its greatest leaders, these details would have been inconvenient.
But Scripture includes them.
Because its ultimate hero is not Moses.
It is not Aaron.
It is not Jochebed.
It is the Lord who remains faithful even when human beings prove painfully unfaithful.
And that truth should humble every one of us.
Because sometimes we are quick to celebrate grace when we need it and equally quick to withhold compassion when someone else's history makes us uncomfortable.
We praise God for forgiving our secret sins while quietly assuming another person's family scandal has permanently ruined their future.
We tell people that Jesus changes lives, then act as though certain people are too damaged to be changed.
We preach redemption until the person needing redemption has a story that embarrasses us.
But the Gospel confronts that hypocrisy.
It does not say that sin is harmless.
It does not say that every relationship is holy.
It does not say that consequences disappear simply because someone believes in God.
It says something far more powerful.
Sin is serious enough that Christ had to die, and God's mercy is great enough that sinners who come to Christ can truly be forgiven and transformed.
And this is where the story of Aaron becomes especially important.
Because Aaron's priesthood was not the final answer to humanity's deepest problem.
It was pointing forward to Someone greater.
The high priests of Israel were themselves sinners.
They needed sacrifices for their own sins as well as for the sins of the people.
Hebrews 5:3 explains this weakness.
And Hebrews 7:27 reveals the glorious contrast.
Jesus Christ does not need to offer sacrifices for His own sins.
He has none.
He is the sinless High Priest who offered Himself once for all.
The Greek of Hebrews 7:26 describes Him as:
"ἅγιος ἄκακος ἀμίαντος"
Hagios, akakos, amiantos.
"Holy, innocent, unstained."
These words describe the moral purity of Jesus Christ.
Aaron came from a complicated family history and personally failed.
Jesus entered human history without sin.
Aaron's priesthood was temporary.
Christ's priesthood is eternal.
Aaron offered the blood of sacrificial animals.
Jesus offered His own blood.
Aaron could represent the people before God, but he could not permanently remove their sin.
Jesus Christ, through His once-for-all sacrifice, accomplished what the repeated sacrifices of the old covenant could never accomplish.
Hebrews 7:25 declares:
"Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them." — KJV
To the uttermost.
Not halfway.
Not until your past becomes embarrassing.
Not until someone reminds you where you came from.
Not until your mistakes become too public.
Christ is able to save completely those who come to God through Him.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this has needed to hear for years.
Because you have been trying to outrun a history you cannot change.
You have changed your appearance.
Changed your surroundings.
Changed your circle of friends.
Maybe even changed the way you speak about your childhood.
But when the room becomes quiet, you still hear those old accusations.
You know where you came from.
You know what your family did.
You know what you have done.
People like you do not become people God uses.
But the Gospel does not tell you to rewrite the facts of your past.
It calls you to bring the truth into the light before the Savior who redeems sinners.
You do not need to pretend that evil was good.
You do not need to excuse what God condemns.
You do not need to make peace with sin.
You need Jesus Christ.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not limited to people with respectable family histories.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned up every part of our lives.
Not after we convinced everyone that our family was respectable.
Not after we became worthy of salvation.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
But do not mistake grace for permission to remain unchanged.
The same Jesus who receives sinners calls them to repentance.
The same Savior who forgives also transforms.
The same Lord who welcomes the broken commands His people to walk in holiness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not God pretending that sin does not matter.
Grace is God providing, through Jesus Christ, the forgiveness and new life that sinners could never earn for themselves.
And this is why the story of Amram and Jochebed must not be turned into a slogan that says, "God blessed a forbidden marriage, so our choices do not matter."
That would be a misuse of the passage.
The Bible does not present their marriage as a pattern Christians should imitate.
The later prohibition in Leviticus must be taken seriously.
But neither should their family history be used to suggest that Moses and Aaron were somehow beyond God's reach.
Both extremes miss the point.
God's holiness remains holy.
His mercy remains mercy.
And His sovereign purposes are not defeated by the brokenness of the human families through which He works.
Perhaps you are reading this as a parent who carries regret.
You know there were moments when your children suffered because of your decisions.
You cannot return to those years.
You cannot unsay the words.
You cannot undo every consequence.
But you can repent.
You can confess what was wrong.
You can seek forgiveness without demanding it.
You can begin living differently.
And you can entrust your children to the God whose power is not limited by your failures.
Perhaps you are the child of such a parent.
You have spent years carrying embarrassment for things you never chose.
Listen carefully.
You are responsible for your own response to God, but you are not personally guilty merely because of the sins of your parents.
Ezekiel 18:20 makes clear that a son does not bear the guilt of his father simply by being his son.
Your ancestry is part of your history.
It is not the final verdict on your soul.
And if you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not found in the scandal attached to your surname.
It is found in the Savior who purchased your redemption.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — KJV
Notice those words.
In Christ.
Not merely in a religious family.
Not merely in church attendance.
Not merely in good intentions.
In Christ.
The new creation is not a promise that every earthly consequence will disappear or that every painful memory will instantly stop hurting.
It is the reality of a new life and relationship with God through union with Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the first evidence of that new life is not a dramatic public miracle.
Sometimes it is a quiet confession.
A long-overdue apology.
A decision to stop lying.
A refusal to repeat the cruelty you grew up witnessing.
A willingness to forgive without pretending the harm never happened.
A return to prayer after years of running from God.
Sometimes transformation begins with a trembling voice whispering:
"Lord Jesus, I cannot change where I came from. But I surrender who I am becoming to You."
And if those words describe your heart today, do not merely admire the idea of grace.
Respond to the Savior who offers it.
Turn from your sin.
Trust in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Ask Him for forgiveness.
Follow Him as Lord.
Not because your past is insignificant.
But because His saving power is greater than your ability to rescue yourself.
And now, return with me to that ancient family in Egypt.
Amram.
Jochebed.
Miriam.
Aaron.
Moses.
A genealogy that raises difficult questions.
A mother who placed her baby in a basket.
A sister who watched from the riverbank.
A son who confronted Pharaoh.
A brother who became high priest.
A people delivered from slavery.
And centuries later, a greater Deliverer would come.
Not merely to lead people out of Egypt.
But to redeem people from sin.
Not merely to stand before an earthly king.
But to reconcile sinners to the living God.
Not merely to serve as a priest for one generation.
But to reign as the eternal High Priest who ever lives to intercede for His people.
That Deliverer is Jesus Christ.
And the deepest beauty of this story is not that an unusual marriage produced two remarkable sons.
It is that the Bible's long story of redemption leads beyond every imperfect human instrument to the only perfectly righteous Savior.
Moses could lead Israel through the sea, but only Jesus can bring sinners into everlasting reconciliation with God.
Aaron could enter the earthly sanctuary, but Jesus entered heaven itself on behalf of His people.
Jochebed could place her son into a basket and hope for his preservation, but God gave His Son for the salvation of all who believe.
And suddenly the ancient genealogy is no longer merely an uncomfortable detail.
It becomes another reminder of how desperately humanity needs a Redeemer.
Maybe this article found you while you were quietly struggling with shame.
Maybe you have been hiding a part of your story because you are afraid people would treat you differently if they knew.
Maybe you have been standing at the edge of faith, convinced that God would never welcome someone with your history.
Please do not confuse the judgment of imperfect people with the invitation of Jesus Christ.
He does not call you to come with a fabricated history.
He calls you to come in repentance and faith.
And He is not asking you to save yourself before you come.
He is the Savior.
If this truth has reached a place in your heart that you have kept hidden, I want to invite you to do something simple and sincere.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose anyone else's sins.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to invite another believer to pray with you.
Someone who has almost given up may need to hear that following Christ is still possible after a painful beginning.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message.
Someone who grew up believing they were an accident.
Someone who thinks their parents' mistakes made them worthless.
Someone who believes their own failures have placed them beyond forgiveness.
Not merely to spread an interesting biblical fact, but to help another person encounter the truth of God's holiness, Christ's forgiveness, and the hope of a transformed life.
Return to it when shame begins speaking louder than Scripture, or when you need to remember the difference between God's approval of a person's actions and His power to redeem a person's life.
We want to help believers grow beyond inspirational quotations into a deeper understanding of God's Word, the Gospel of Jesus Christ, repentance, holiness, grace, and faithful discipleship.
There is a difference between enjoying a message and helping make it possible for more people to receive biblical teaching.
Every article requires time, study, preparation, and care. Continuing this work, improving its quality, and reaching more people require practical support.
The Bible encourages believers to support faithful Gospel work.
Galatians 6:6 teaches that those who receive instruction in the Word should share good things with those who teach.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
But I want to be careful here, because honoring God requires more than making a persuasive appeal.

Some believers may prayerfully choose to give from funds they have set aside for Christian ministry and generosity. Others may need to prioritize their family responsibilities, local church, or other needs.
What matters is that any gift be made freely, responsibly, and with a sincere desire to honor Christ.
It helps sustain the work of preparing more articles, sharing biblical teaching, encouraging struggling believers, and expanding access to discipleship resources.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply additional ways to encourage believers and express appreciation for those who help sustain the ministry.
The greater purpose remains unchanged.
More people opening their Bibles.
More believers growing in discernment.
More wounded hearts hearing the truth of the Gospel.
More families learning to follow Jesus.
More Christians becoming rooted in Scripture rather than carried away by every passing message.
Our desire is not to put spiritual nourishment beyond the reach of people who cannot afford it.
It is to keep sharing biblical resources while inviting those who are able and willing to help sustain and expand the work.
It would be a sinner turning to Christ.
A believer returning to the Word.
A wounded person finding courage to seek help and healing.
A proud heart humbled by the holiness of God.
A struggling disciple remembering that Jesus is still worthy of trust.
And before you leave, I want you to remember one final thing.
When Exodus tells us that Amram married his aunt Jochebed, Scripture does not invite us to celebrate a relationship that God's Law would later forbid.
It invites us to read the Bible carefully, honestly, and in its redemptive context.
When we encounter Moses and Aaron, we are not looking at men whose family history made them morally superior.
We are looking at human beings whose lives demonstrate the need for God's mercy and whose ministries ultimately point beyond themselves.
Beyond Moses stands the greater Mediator.
Beyond Aaron stands the greater High Priest.
Beyond every broken family tree stands the One who offers sinners a new life through His death and resurrection.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing about His invitation is that you do not have to erase your history before you come to Him.
You have to come truthfully.
Repentantly.
Trusting Him.
Ready to follow.
Because your family's past may explain some of the pain you carry, but it cannot determine the limits of Christ's power to redeem you.
The people who remember where you came from may never let you forget your past—but the Savior who knows everything about you can still give you a future that belongs to Him.
